monks
------------------------------------------
See MONASTICISM, SAṀNYĀSA and YATI.

Monasticism
------------------------------------------
Introduction
‘Great things can be done by great sacrifices only’ avers Vivekānanda (A. D. 1863-1902). No wonder then, that, in order to attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmi-gratory existence—which is an extremely arduous task—great effort is needed. This presupposes freedom from the bondages, duties and responsibilities of worldly life or family life. Hence त्याग or renunciation and तपस् or austerities—in short, asceticism—are often stressed in the Hindu scriptures.
Mokṣa has been declared as the birth-right of every human being and not the prerogative of only a handful of persons. The very purpose of the puruṣārtha concept and the आश्रम scheme of life is to afford an opportunity for everyone to try for मोक्ष (See ĀŚRAMA and PURUṢĀRTHAS.).
In the वेदस् and the Upaniṣads
Asceticism was not unknown to the वेदस्. In the Ṛgveda (10.136.2) there is a reference to the munis. They put on dirty garments and had great psychic powers. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (2.23.1) refers to the brahmacāri who remains celibate throughout his life and lives in his गुरु’s होउसे, studying the scriptures. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.5.1) clearly refers to the ṛṣis who had known the आत्मन्, to have renounced the world and taken to a mendicant’s life. Some minor उपनिषद्स् like the Mahānārāyaṇa (10.5) and the Kaivalya (1.3) state how some aspirants attained इम्मोर्तलित्य् by renouncing the world and worldly life. Other उपनिषद्स् (from among them) like the Nāradaparivrājaka, the Paramahaṁsa and the Bhikṣuka deal directly with the monastic life.
The Two Paths
Though मोक्ष was posited before the human beings as the final goal of life, the Hindu sages knew that all were not equally competent to pursue it vigorously and consciously. Hence they offered two paths to reach the goal—the pravṛttimārga (path of activism) and the निवृत्तिमार्ग (path of detachment)—both of which, if properly understood and assiduously practised, will lead to the same goal.
In the former way of life, a person was free to marry, raise a family and fulfill all the legitimate desires of the body and the मिन्द्, as per the dictates of the śāstras (the holy scriptures) and the codes of धर्म (righteous living). In this stage of life, called ‘gārhasthya’, great stress was also laid upon the social responsibilities to be discharged by the couple and the family as a whole.
As the person passes through the various experiences of life, both good and bad, वैराग्य (disinterestedness through the maturing of wisdom) will rise in his मिन्द्, making him gradually withdraw from the family life and turn his attention more and more towards the higher, the spiritual, values of life. This in essence, is निवृत्तिमार्ग, even though the person may not formally take to the वानप्रस्थ or the सṁन्यास आश्रम.
In the निवृत्तिमार्ग, a person may take to सṁन्यास or the last stage of life even from the first (or the second) without going through the other stages or āśramas, an intense feeling of वैराग्य (the spirit of renunciation) being the only criterion.
Asceticism and Monasticism
Asceticism (or तपस्) in life was a common phenomenon even in the Vedic days. Anyone interested in spiritual welfare or even in achieving something which could not be got by ordinary human means, was advised to undergo तपस् or austerities, the intensity of which depended upon the greatness of the goal desired to be achieved. For instance, the sage भृगु, वरुण’s son, was advised to perform तपस् to know ब्रह्मन् (vide Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). हिरण्यकशिपु, the king of the राक्षसस् or demons, undertook तपस् to achieve greater powers to conquer the देवस् or the gods in हेअवेन् (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.17.2; Bhāgavata 7.3). So also रावण, the king of लङ्का (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇda 9 and 10).
Though asceticism does not necessarily include मोनस्तिचिस्म्, it is an integral part of the latter. A saṁnyāsin or a monk is permitted to accept only the bare necessities of life like a kaupīna (loin-cloth), kanthā (wrapper), दण्ड (stick), कमण्डलु (water-pot), pādukā (wooden footwear) and śikya (cloth hung over the shoulder, for collecting alms). These are necessary for the sustenance of the body so that he can practise spiritual disciplines in a better frame of मिन्द्.
Organised Monasticism
Though सṁन्यास (monastic life) was prescribed as the last stage of life and though individual मोन्क्स् did exist in the Hindu society over the millennia, organised मोनस्तिचिस्म् owes its origin to शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820). Of course, it already existed in बुद्धिस्म् and जैनिस्म्.
Śaṅkara established four chief mona-steries in the four cardinal directions of India—Jyotir मठ near Badarī in the north, Kālikā मठ at द्वारका in the west, गोवर्धन मठ at पुरी in the east and Śṛṅgerī Śāradāpīṭha at Śṛṅgerī in the south. He also appointed four of his disciples as the first pontiffs of these four monasteries.
Later, other monastic and ascetic orders also came into existence.
List of Monastic and Ascetic Orders
Over the centuries several ascetic orders have come into existence, some of which are monastic and the others, not. They may be dealt with very briefly as follows:
The Aghorapanthīs are the अस्चेतिच्स् of a queer Śaiva order who worship शिव as ‘Aghora’ (the ‘non-terrible’) but practise abominable things like cannibalism and eating from a human skull and so on. See AGHORAPANTHĪ for details.
The अलख्नामीस् are a sect of śūdra अस्चेतिच्स् living mostly in Rajasthan. They are gentle by nature and practise non-violence.
(See ALAKHNĀMĪS for details.)
The दशनामीस् are saṁnyāsins of the advaita school, established by शङ्कर. They are ten in number (as the very name suggests), attached to the four principal maṭhas. (See DAŚANĀMĪS for details.)
The Kālāmukhās are a sect of अस्चेतिच्स् belonging to the Śaiva order. They are so called since they deface their faces with black marks and symbols. They belong to the नकुलीश-पाशुपत cult.
The Kāpālikas are also अस्चेतिच्स् of Śaiva cult using the कपाल or the human skull as a begging bowl. Hence the name. (See ŚAIVISM.)
The Nāgā-साधुस् are a militant sect of saṁnyāsins of the daśanāmī group organised by मधुसूदन सरस्वती (A. D. 1525-1632). Their monasteries are called ‘akhāḍas’.
The Nāthpanthis, also called Jogīs, are the followers of मत्स्येन्द्रनाथ and Gorakṣanātha (Gorakhnāth). They concentrate on हठयोग and are vehemently opposed to association with women in any form.
The Nirmalas are a sect of reformist अस्चेतिच्स् more akin to सिखिस्म्. They accept the worship of the five Hindu gods—Śiva, विष्णु, देवी, गणपति and Sūrya—revere the Granth Sāhib and consider that Rām and Rahīm are the names of the same Supreme God.
The Rāmānandis are saṁnyāsins belonging to the order established by रामानन्द (birth A. D. 1300). They call their Vaiṣṇava tradition as ‘Śrīsampra-dāya’. Their tutelary deity is सीता. Their centres are known as ‘dvāras’.
The Udāsis are a sect of monistic saṁnyāsins started by Śrīcand (A. D. 1494-1629), the elder son of गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539). They accept the authority of the वेदस् and worship the five deities (pañcāyatana पूजा). In addition, they revere गुरु Nānak and the Grantha Sāhib. That is why they are also known as Nānakśāhis or Nānakpanthīs.
The Vairāgis (or Bairāgis) are a sect of Vaiṣṇava अस्चेतिच्स् who wear white robes and the ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र (vertical religious mark) on their foreheads. They may grow beard and keep their hair matted. Four traditions or orders are recognised among them.
Modern Orders of Monasticism
Among the modern editions of ancient and traditional मोनस्तिचिस्म्, the most important one is the Ramakrishna Order. Modern but simple way of living, community life, preaching work combined with social service activities distinguish it from the traditional मोनस्तिचिस्म्. A parallel order for women—of saṁnyāsinīs—has also been started since 1956.
Conclusion
Monasticism as a way of life is still very much in vogue in the Hindu society. The fact that many highly educated young men and women are opting for this life shows that it is still vibrant and a force to reckon with.
